hmmt-nov-2015-thm-01.title: Similar triangles
hmmt-nov-2015-thm-01.body:
Let the vertices go around the square in order $A,B,C,D$. Let line $BE$ meet line $AD$ at $Q$. Since $E$ is the midpoint of $CD$ and $BC\parallel DQ$, triangles $ECB$ and $EDQ$ are congruent, so $DQ=BC=1$ and $AQ=AD+DQ=2$.

Because $AQ\parallel BF$, triangles $APQ$ and $FPB$ are similar, so $\frac{AP}{PF}=\frac{AQ}{BF}=\frac{2}{2/3}=3$.

**Answer: 3**

hmmt-nov-2015-thm-01.title: Coordinates
hmmt-nov-2015-thm-01.body:
Take $A=(0,0)$, $B=(1,0)$, $C=(1,1)$, $D=(0,1)$. Then $E=(\tfrac12,1)$ and $F=(1,\tfrac23)$. Line $AF$: $(t,\tfrac23t)$. Line $BE$: $(1-\tfrac s2,s)$. Setting $\tfrac23t=s$ and $t=1-\tfrac s2$ gives $t=1-\tfrac t3$, so $t=\tfrac34$. Hence $AP=\tfrac34AF$ and $PF=\tfrac14AF$, ratio $3$.

**Answer: 3**

hmmt-nov-2015-thm-02.title: Factor a sum
hmmt-nov-2015-thm-02.body:
Let the grid be $\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{smallmatrix}$. The products are $ab,cd,ac,bd$. The total is
$$a+b+c+d+ab+cd+ac+bd=(a+d)+(b+c)+(a+d)(b+c)=2015,$$
so $(a+d+1)(b+c+1)=2016$ (here $a+d$ and $b+c$ are the two diagonals; the row and column products add to $(a+d)(b+c)$).

We minimise $(a+d+1)+(b+c+1)-2$ for a fixed product $2016$, so we want the two factors as close as possible. $\sqrt{2016}\approx44.9$, and the nearest divisor pair is $42\cdot48$. So the sum of the four numbers is $42+48-2=88$ (achievable, e.g. $a=d$ chosen to sum to $41$ and $b,c$ to sum to $47$ with positive integers).

**Answer: 88**

hmmt-nov-2015-thm-03.title: Circumradius
hmmt-nov-2015-thm-03.body:
The three inscribed circles have radius $\frac12$ and centres $A=(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$, $B=(\tfrac32,\tfrac52)$, $C=(\tfrac52,\tfrac32)$. The circle $O$ is externally tangent to all three, so its centre is equidistant from $A,B,C$ and $r+\frac12=R$, the circumradius of $ABC$.

$BC=\sqrt2$, $AB=AC=\sqrt5$. The altitude from $A$ is $\sqrt{5-\tfrac12}=\tfrac{3\sqrt2}{2}$, so the area is $\tfrac12\cdot\sqrt2\cdot\tfrac{3\sqrt2}{2}=\tfrac32$. Then
$$R=\frac{BC\cdot CA\cdot AB}{4[ABC]}=\frac{\sqrt2\cdot5}{6}=\frac{5\sqrt2}{6}.$$
So $r=\frac{5\sqrt2}{6}-\frac12=\frac{5\sqrt2-3}{6}$.

**Answer: $\frac{5\sqrt2-3}{6}$**

hmmt-nov-2015-thm-04.title: Crowley can hold the score to 6
hmmt-nov-2015-thm-04.body:
Number the rows $1$ to $4$ from the top. Crowley pairs each square of row $2$ with the square directly below it in row $3$, and answers as follows: if Aziraphale colours a square in row $2$ (or $3$), Crowley colours its partner in row $3$ (or $2$); if Aziraphale colours a square in row $1$ (or $4$), Crowley colours any other uncoloured square of the same row (there always is one, since each row has an even number of squares and moves in it come in pairs).

Now every vertical link between rows $2$ and $3$ contains a blue square, so every red region lies inside the top half (rows $1,2$) or the bottom half (rows $3,4$). In one half Aziraphale can have all $4$ squares of the middle row, but only $2$ of the $4$ squares of the outer row. So the largest red region has at most $4+2=6$ squares.

**Upper bound: 6**

hmmt-nov-2015-thm-04.title: Aziraphale can force 6
hmmt-nov-2015-thm-04.body:
Aziraphale starts with two adjacent central squares; this is always possible on his first two turns. If Crowley lets him have a third central square, he is adjacent to at least seven uncoloured squares and can add two more touching red squares, and since Crowley owns at most as many squares as Aziraphale, one more after that, reaching $6$. If Crowley blocks the remaining centre squares, Aziraphale continues along the same inner row: either he takes both ends, giving a row of four with two attached squares, or after Crowley takes one end he takes a square in the outer row next to his chain, still leaving four free squares next to red ones of which he gets half, so at least $4+\tfrac42=6$ red squares in one connected region.

An exhaustive computer search of the whole game tree gives the game value $6$, confirming both bounds.

**Answer: 6**

hmmt-nov-2015-thm-05.title: Upper bound
hmmt-nov-2015-thm-05.body:
Swapping rows or columns does not change whether four red squares form a rectangle. Assume the top row has the most red squares, $k$ of them, and (by permuting columns) they are the first $k$ columns.

In those $k$ columns, each of the other four rows has at most one red square (two would form a rectangle with the top row), giving at most $k+4$ red squares. In the other $5-k$ columns the top row is empty, so at most $4(5-k)$ red squares. Total $\le (k+4)+4(5-k)=24-3k$. If at least $13$ squares were red then $13\le24-3k$, so $k\le3$: every row has at most $3$ red squares. With at least $13$ red squares, at least three rows have exactly $3$.

Take three rows with exactly $3$ red squares each; any two share at most one red column. Say the first has columns $\{1,2,3\}$. The second shares at most one of them, so it contains both columns $4$ and $5$. The third has three columns, at most one from $\{1,2,3\}$, so it also contains both $4$ and $5$, and then rows two and three share two columns: a rectangle. This contradiction shows at most $12$.

**Upper bound: 12**

hmmt-nov-2015-thm-05.title: Construction with 12
hmmt-nov-2015-thm-05.body:
Colour these squares (R = red), rows top to bottom:

- `R R R . .`
- `R . . R R`
- `. R . R .`
- `. R . . R`
- `. . R R .`

Any two rows share at most one red column (row sets $\{1,2,3\},\{1,4,5\},\{2,4\},\{2,5\},\{3,4\}$ intersect pairwise in at most one element), so no rectangle appears. That is $3+3+2+2+2=12$ red squares.

**Answer: 12**

hmmt-nov-2015-thm-06.title: Count squares
hmmt-nov-2015-thm-06.body:
There are $\binom{36}{4}$ ways to choose four cells. Count tilted and axis-parallel squares whose vertices are cell centres. Each such square is inscribed in a unique axis-parallel square of lattice points (its bounding box), and an $m\times m$ bounding box (side $m$ in centre spacing, so $m=1,\dots,5$) contains exactly $m$ such squares (one for each way to cut the sides in ratio $j:m-j$, $j=0,\dots,m-1$), and there are $(6-m)^2$ positions for it.

The total is $\sum_{m=1}^{5}m(6-m)^2=25+32+27+16+5=105$.

The probability is $\frac{105}{\binom{36}{4}}=\frac{105}{58905}=\frac1{561}$.

**Answer: $\frac1{561}$**

hmmt-nov-2015-thm-07.title: Cycle types
hmmt-nov-2015-thm-07.body:
Row $k+1$ is $f^k$ applied to the top row, so we need $f^6=\mathrm{id}$ but $f^k\ne\mathrm{id}$ for $k=1,\dots,5$. So $f$ is a permutation whose cycle lengths divide $6$ and have lcm exactly $6$. The partitions of $7$ into parts from $\{1,2,3,6\}$ with lcm $6$ are $6+1$, $3+2+2$ and $3+2+1+1$.

- $6+1$: choose the fixed point ($7$ ways) and arrange the rest in a $6$-cycle ($5!=120$ ways): $840$.
- $3+2+2$: choose the $3$-cycle's elements $\binom73=35$, its orientation $2$, and split the other four into two $2$-cycles ($3$ ways): $35\cdot2\cdot3=210$.
- $3+2+1+1$: choose the $3$-cycle $\binom73=35$ with $2$ orientations, then the $2$-cycle $\binom42=6$: $35\cdot2\cdot6=420$.

Total $840+210+420=1470$.

**Answer: 1470**

hmmt-nov-2015-thm-08.title: Two classes of squares
hmmt-nov-2015-thm-08.body:
Squares on the top row or right column (other than the target) all have the same expected time $E_e$ by symmetry (swapping rows or columns does not change the movement); every other square has expected time $E_c$. There are $14$ moves from any square.

From a non-edge square, $2$ of the $14$ moves land on an edge square next to the corner line (the squares in the top row and right column in its own row and column): $E_c=\frac2{14}(E_e+1)+\frac{12}{14}(E_c+1)$.

From an edge square: $1$ move hits the target, $6$ moves stay on the edge, $7$ moves go to a non-edge square: $E_e=\frac1{14}(1)+\frac6{14}(E_e+1)+\frac7{14}(E_c+1)$.

Solving: $E_c=E_e+7$ from the first, and then $E_e=63$, $E_c=70$. The rook starts on a non-edge square, so the answer is $70$ (confirmed by solving the full $64$-state linear system).

**Answer: 70**

hmmt-nov-2015-thm-09.title: Track a single digit
hmmt-nov-2015-thm-09.body:
Here "$3\times3$ subsquare" means every $3\times3$ window of the grid, not only the nine disjoint blocks. Suppose a grid has all these properties and write $(r,c)$ for row $r$, column $c$.

The windows with columns $1$-$3$ and columns $2$-$4$ (same rows $1$-$3$) both contain all nine digits, so the three cells $(1,1),(2,1),(3,1)$ hold the same set of digits as $(1,4),(2,4),(3,4)$. Likewise (shifting rows) $(1,1),(1,2),(1,3)$ hold the same digits as $(4,1),(4,2),(4,3)$.

Let $a$ be the digit in $(1,1)$. Then $a$ appears among $(1,4),(2,4),(3,4)$, but not at $(1,4)$ (same row), so at $(2,4)$ or $(3,4)$. Also $a$ appears among $(4,1),(4,2),(4,3)$, but not at $(4,1)$ (same column), so at $(4,2)$ or $(4,3)$. Both of these cells lie in the window of rows $2$-$4$ and columns $2$-$4$, which then contains $a$ twice. Contradiction, so no such grid exists.

**Answer: 0**

hmmt-nov-2015-thm-10.title: Sum the travel distances
hmmt-nov-2015-thm-10.body:
The pigeon eats ten times, and the burrito is thrown $9$ times, so it visits squares $p_1=(0,0)$ and nine further squares $p_2,\dots,p_{10}$, each uniform on the grid ($p_{i+1}$ is uniform independent of $p_i$). Starting with the pigeon on the burrito, each throw to a square at taxicab distance $d_i$ costs exactly $d_i$ minutes of walking (any shortest route) plus $1$ minute of eating.

So the expected total is $1+E\big[\sum_{i=1}^{9}(d_i+1)\big]=10+2\,E\Big[\sum_{i=1}^9|x_{i+1}-x_i|\Big]$ by symmetry of the coordinates. Here $E|x_2-0|=4.5$ (the first throw starts from $p_1=(0,0)$) and for two independent uniform coordinates in $\{0,\dots,9\}$, $E|x-x'|=\frac1{100}\sum_{k=1}^{9}2k(10-k)=3.3$. So the total is $10+2(4.5+8\cdot3.3)=71.8$.

**Answer: 71.8**
